lessons.materials-handling-overview:
**Materials Handling Safety Overview**

Materials handling includes lifting, carrying, pushing, pulling, lowering, stacking, storing, transporting, and securing loads. Injuries can occur during both manual handling and equipment-assisted handling, including back strains, sprains, cuts, pinches, slips, and struck-by incidents. OSHA 1910 Subpart N and 1910.176 establish safe handling, storage, and movement requirements for general industry. Rushing increases the chance of poor judgment and unsafe shortcuts. Safe handling protects employees, equipment, materials, and productivity. When unsure how to handle a material, stop and ask a supervisor before proceeding.
lessons.ppe-for-materials-handling:
**PPE for Materials Handling**

The PPE required for materials handling depends on the materials, work environment, and specific task. Gloves protect hands from splinters, sharp edges, staples, and pinch points but must allow a secure grip. Safety shoes protect feet from dropped objects. Eye protection may be needed where dust, chips, or particles are present. Clothing should allow full movement without being so loose it can catch on equipment. Always inspect PPE before use and replace damaged items. PPE reduces injury severity but does not replace safe work practices.
lessons.ergonomics-body-mechanics:
**Ergonomic Hazards and Body Mechanics**

Twisting while lifting is one of the most common causes of back injuries. Ergonomic risk factors include twisting at the waist, bending forward repeatedly, overreaching, lifting above shoulder height, and performing repetitive motions without breaks. To reduce ergonomic strain, pivot with your feet instead of twisting at the waist, keep materials close to your body, use step stools or ladders for elevated items, and take periodic breaks. Repetitive motion can lead to long-term musculoskeletal injuries. OSHA expects employers to protect workers from recognized ergonomic hazards.
lessons.planning-the-lift:
**Planning the Lift or Move**

Before moving any material, identify the destination, choose the safest route, and clear obstacles from the travel path. Inspect the object for labels such as Top Heavy, Fragile, or hazard warnings indicating special precautions. Check the load for sharp edges, splinters, staples, leaking contents, or poor handholds. Test the weight before committing to the lift. Decide whether the load can be handled safely alone or whether help or mechanical assistance is needed. A safe move begins before the load leaves the ground.
lessons.lifting-carrying-techniques:
**Proper Lifting, Carrying, and Lowering Techniques**

Stand close to the load with feet shoulder-width apart. Bend at the knees, not at the waist. Keep your back as straight as possible, get a firm grip, and hold the load close to your body. Lift smoothly with your legs. When carrying, keep the load close, keep elbows slightly bent, and ensure clear visibility ahead. Never carry a load that blocks your view — use a cart, reduce the load, or get help. When lowering, bend at the knees, keep your back straight, and watch your fingers. Do not jerk the load, twist while lifting, or reach far out to set a load down.
lessons.awkward-loads-team-lifting:
**Awkward Loads and Team Lifting**

Awkward loads — long, bulky, slippery, or difficult to grip — require extra planning. Inspect awkward loads for safe handholds and balance the load before carrying. Use equipment for loads that are too heavy or awkward to handle safely alone. When two or more people lift together, one person should direct all movements. Everyone must know when to lift, when to move, when to stop, and when to lower the load. Clear communication before and during a team lift prevents injury. Asking for help is a safe work practice, not a sign of weakness.
lessons.handling-aids:
**Hand Trucks, Carts, and Handling Aids**

Use handling aids — hand trucks, carts, dollies, pallet jacks — when manual handling is unsafe. Inspect equipment before every use for damaged wheels, loose parts, broken handles, or missing safety devices. Remove damaged equipment from service and report defects to a supervisor. When using hand trucks, load materials flush against the back plate and do not stack above the handhold. Load carts with heavier items on the bottom. Push rather than pull whenever possible for better control and reduced strain. Keep loads stable and within capacity, and return equipment to designated storage after use.
lessons.pallets-pallet-jacks:
**Pallets, Pallet Jacks, and Scissor-Lift Tables**

Inspect pallets for damage before use and load them evenly with heavier items on the bottom. Keep loads within equipment capacity and avoid stacking so high that visibility is blocked or loads become unstable. Secure unstable pallet loads with stretch wrap or straps before moving. When using pallet jacks, insert forks carefully, lift only enough to clear the floor, and move slowly. Scissor-lift tables reduce bending and reaching but introduce pinch-point hazards — keep hands and body parts clear of the scissor mechanism. A load that appears stable at rest may shift once in motion; always inspect and secure it before transport.
lessons.powered-equipment:
**Powered Equipment and Forklift Awareness**

Only trained and authorized employees may operate powered industrial trucks, including forklifts and powered pallet trucks, as required by the employer's program. Operators must inspect equipment before use, confirm loads are within rated capacity, and ensure loads are stable and secure. Forklift loads should generally be carried low and tilted back when appropriate. Operators must obey facility speed limits, traffic patterns, and pedestrian safety rules. Employees working near powered equipment must stay alert, avoid walking under raised loads, make eye contact with operators when crossing paths, and follow site traffic rules.
lessons.special-materials:
**Hazardous, Special, and Unusual Materials**

Some materials require special handling due to their shape, contents, pressure, or hazard classification. Compressed gas cylinders must never be hand-rolled or dragged; use approved cylinder carts that secure the cylinder during transport. Hazardous materials may require special PPE, labeling, handling procedures, and spill response protocols — always read labels and follow workplace procedures before handling. Drums, fragile items, top-heavy loads, and other special materials may require approved attachments or supervisor direction. When handling requirements are unclear, stop and ask a supervisor rather than guessing.
